transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I spend a lot of time down at the local museum. I help out there a lot since I stopped working. The historical society runs it, and they just put in this beautiful new exhibit on the old railroad. My grandfather actually worked on that railroad, you know, back in the twenties. They used to have these massive steam engines come right through the center of town, it was really something. 

But, uh, anyway, what I was saying is... the problem is that people at the museum will be talking right to me, like about organizing the next art walk. And I’ll be looking right at them, but then I realize I completely missed the middle of what they just said. I have to stop them and ask them to run it by me again. It's getting a bit embarrassing. The art walk usually gets a huge turnout, especially when the weather is nice, so we have to coordinate with all the local cafes and shops, but I just... I keep losing track of what people are saying when they're standing right in front of me.
Have you had this kind of trouble paying attention since you were a child?

Well, yeah, I suppose I have. Even way back in grade school, I remember my report cards always said things like “daydreams” or “needs reminders to finish work.” I went to Lincoln Elementary, actually, right over on Elm Street. They tore it down a few years ago to build that new strip mall, which is a real shame because it had this beautiful old brickwork on the front. My buddy Tom and I used to play stickball against the side of the gymnasium there every afternoon. Tom actually just moved down to Florida last month—says the warm weather is better for his knees, though I can't stand the humidity myself. 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right, school. Yeah, my mother used to have to sit right beside me at the kitchen table just to keep me on track with my homework. This was before I was twelve or so. She’d be cooking dinner—she made the absolute best pot roast, with those little pearl onions and the potatoes that would get all soft in the gravy—and she'd just have to keep reaching over and tapping my textbook to get me to actually finish my assignments.
Have these attention and memory problems been getting worse more recently, or have they stayed about the same over time?

Well, they've always been there, like I was saying, but... I guess it’s been noticeably causing a lot more trouble for about two years and four months now. That was right around the time my friend Arthur passed away. He was the one who usually handled the museum liaison duties, and we did a lot of it together. Poor Arthur, it was his heart... just gave out on him while he was mowing the front lawn. He had this old riding mower, a John Deere, one of the really sturdy ones from the eighties. You just don't see craftsmanship like that anymore, everything is plastic now. I actually tried to buy it from his widow, but her son wanted it for his property up north. They get a lot of snow up there, though, so I don't know how much use he actually gets out of a riding mower... 

But, uh, anyway... where was I? Oh, right. Since Arthur died, I had to take over all those museum liaison duties by myself. And without him there to kind of catch the things I missed or remind me what people said, it's just become really obvious that I'm struggling to keep track of it all. So yeah, it's definitely been worse since then.
Since these problems got worse, have they kept gradually getting worse over time?

Well, I wouldn't say they've kept getting worse, no. It's more like... it's just been a steady struggle since I took over for Arthur. It hasn't really changed since then. Though, speaking of Arthur, his widow, Martha, she just started coming back to the museum meetings last week. It was nice to see her. She brought these incredible oatmeal raisin cookies she makes. She uses a touch of molasses in the batter, makes them really chewy, you know? She used to bring them to all the historical society bake sales. We used to raise so much money with those bake sales, enough to fix the roof on the old depot building back in 2018. The shingles were practically falling off every time we had a strong wind... 

But, uh... I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Oh, right, getting worse. No, no, it's pretty much just stayed at this same level of... well, just being a real hassle, honestly, since I've been doing it all on my own.
Before age 12, did you often have trouble staying focused on schoolwork or following instructions?

Well, yeah, like I mentioned earlier with my mother helping me at the kitchen table, that was definitely before I was twelve. Following instructions was always a bit of a challenge for me. 

I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She'd stand at the front of the room and give us these long lists of directions for our history projects. We had to make these dioramas in shoeboxes once. I used an old Buster Brown shoebox. My mother used to take me to the shoe store downtown—Miller's Shoes, it was called. Old Mr. Miller had one of those cold metal contraptions he'd slide your foot into to measure your size. He was a nice man, always gave out a little piece of hard candy when you checked out. Usually butterscotch. I'm not a big fan of butterscotch, honestly, it always gets stuck in my teeth, but you didn't want to be rude, you know? My sister loved them, though, so I'd usually just save mine in my pocket for her. She actually still lives in the house we grew up in, if you can believe it. 

Anyway... gosh, I'm sorry, I'm wandering off again. Instructions, right. Yes, by the time Mrs. Gable finished telling us how to build the project, I'd have completely forgotten the first three steps she said. I just couldn't keep my mind on it long enough to take it all in. So yes, I definitely had trouble with that back then.
Have you had any trouble managing everyday tasks like handling money, medications, or other routines that you used to do without a problem?

Handling money and all that? No, not really. I mean, I've got my routine down for paying the bills and keeping track of my medications. I haven't noticed any new problems with that sort of thing. I always sit down on Sunday mornings with my pill organizer—one of those plastic ones with the days of the week on it. Mine has AM and PM slots, though I only really need the AM ones right now. I got it at the pharmacy down the street, the one next to the old movie theater. You know, they're talking about tearing that theater down to build a parking garage. It's a shame, really. I saw my first movie there, "The Sound of Music." My mother took me. We sat right in the middle, and the screen just seemed so huge back then. They had real velvet curtains that they'd pull back before the show started. You just don't get that kind of presentation anymore. Now it's all sticky floors and overpriced popcorn. I read in the paper that the city council is having a big meeting about the parking garage next Tuesday. I might go, actually, just to see what they say... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my routines. Yeah, no, those are all fine. I haven't had any trouble with bills or my pills or anything like that. That's all stayed pretty much the same.
When you forget what someone just said, is it because your mind has wandered off, or do you truly not remember it even right after hearing it?

Well, it's definitely because my mind wanders off. It's not like the words just vanish from my brain, it's more like... I'm listening, and then suddenly I'm thinking about something else entirely. Like the other day, I was at the grocery store, talking to the cashier, Brenda. She's been working there for years, always wears these bright floral aprons. She was telling me about her grandson's little league game, and she mentioned they played at Centennial Park. Well, as soon as she said Centennial Park, I started thinking about the big oak tree they had to cut down there last summer because of the rot. It was a beautiful tree, must have been a hundred years old. We used to have the historical society picnics right under it. We'd set up these long folding tables and everyone would bring a dish. Martha always brought her potato salad, the one with the dill... 

Oh, dear, I'm doing it right now, aren't I? I'm sorry. But yes, that's exactly what happens. My mind just catches on one little thing and off I go, and then I realize I haven't heard a word the person just said. It's not that I can't remember it, I just wasn't really there to hear it in the first place.
Have you started having trouble remembering things that happened recently, like conversations or appointments, even when you were paying attention?

Well, no, if I'm actually tuned in and paying attention, my memory is sharp as a tack. I don't forget things that just happened. Like, I had a dentist appointment last Thursday, remembered it perfectly. Dr. Henderson is my dentist. He’s got this massive saltwater fish tank in his waiting room now. It’s really quite something. There’s this one little yellow fish that always hides behind a plastic diver. We used to have a little freshwater tank when my boys were young. Won a goldfish at the county fair, throwing ping-pong balls into those little glass bowls. You know, they don't even hold the fair at the old fairgrounds anymore. Sold the whole lot to some developer who put up a hundred identical gray townhouses. Every single one has a bright red door. I always tell my neighbor, I don't know how anyone finds their way home in the dark over there, they all look exactly the same. 

But anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, remembering things. No, if I'm focused, I don't have any trouble remembering appointments or what someone just said. It's just the wandering mind that gets me, like I said before. If I actually hear it, I remember it.
